cells.tense: You are shining here because what you tended has come ripe.
cells.act: trace the pattern across the last few times
cells.ask: Think back over the last few times you shared something you love with a group. What did those moments have in common, and what did they leave with people? Name it in one line.
cells.core:
You stand in front of a group and the light you carry is real. It comes from things you actually developed, not from wanting to impress, and you can hand them on without dimming them. When you tell the story of what your people value, it lands, and they lean in because the roots are real.

That's the balance, and there's more you can do with it. Step back far enough to see the whole shape of what you're passing on — not just the words, but how they sit against what came before and what they might grow into. Seeing the pattern underneath makes it clearer. You'll know which parts matter and which are ready to be let go.

cells.tense: You will be promising a dawn that hasn't been earned yet.
cells.act: write the first thing you knew about it, before the reasons
cells.ask: Before you give the reasons for where this is headed, put the first thing you actually knew about it on a note. Keep it nearby.
cells.core:
You feel the pull toward what's bright and it comes out of your mouth as though it's already arrived. The energy is real, but you're stretching it forward over ground you haven't walked, and the brightness is doing some of the work of looking past what's actually there.

Something in you already knows what's solid and what's being forced. That knowing doesn't need your arguments. Before you say another word about where this is going, set down the first thing you knew — before the reasons, before the plan. One honest line is worth more than the whole forecast, and it holds up when the forecast doesn't.

cells.tense: You were tending something that never got to flower.
cells.act: tend it small and ask nothing of it
cells.ask: Pick one small piece of the tradition you care about — one practice, one story — and tend it just for yourself this week. Don't plan what it will become.
cells.core:
You've put time into something that carries meaning for people — a practice, a story, a way of doing things — and it hasn't come to anything you can show. The hope that kept you watering it has gone quiet. You still stand near it, but it sits behind you, like a door you already walked through. The tiredness isn't from laziness; it's from long care that didn't get to ripen.

Start smaller than feels right. Take one piece of it — one practice, one memory, one sentence — and tend it with no purpose beyond the watering. Do it for yourself. Not to rebuild the whole thing, just to feel your hands in it again. Care that doesn't have to become anything is how this kind of tired comes back.

cells.tense: You are already the light here and you don't count it.
cells.act: carry it without tightening around it
cells.ask: Next time you're holding something together for the group — a meeting, a launch, a hard week — notice your grip on it, and set down whatever you're clutching hardest.
cells.core:
People come to you for direction without saying so. You carry what this group values, and you do it so naturally that it doesn't register as work. You might think you're just doing your part, or that someone else is really behind it. The light here is often yours, and you've stopped noticing when it's on or when it's gone out.

Shining harder isn't the move. Feel what you're carrying. Next time you're in the middle of keeping something together, notice your grip on it. Carry it without tightening around it. If you're asked to shrink what you're doing, stay at your real size. Holding steady is not the same as forcing, and the difference shows.

attempts.check: The record supports only that the light is projected forward rather than radiating from what has ripened; it does not say the person is lying to themselves or that others notice the difference, and the Too Much core no longer claims either. The Too Little cell no longer says how long the tending lasted or that it never bloomed — it says the hope has gone quiet and the thing sits behind the person, which is what the record's 'hope defeated by experience' supports. The four asks are now shaped differently: a naming, a note kept, a tending without a plan, a letting go in the moment. The sentence that serves me more than them is the Too Much line about the brightness keeping the ground from being looked at; it reads clever and flatters the diagnosis, so it is now plain.
